items.question: If the stated definition is impossible, does that undermine the causal account?
premises: A definition has been stated for the causal account.
The impossibility of that definition is considered.
The inquiry does not end in mere loss of the cause.
items.inference: Therefore, even if the stated definition fails, the question resolves without abandoning the causal account.
uncertainties: The exact referent of hetumātre depends on the preceding argument.
items.plain_english: So, even if this stated definition is impossible, there is no loss in taking it as a mere cause; rather, the question comes to rest there.

items.question: Can instrumental causes, as opposed to material causes, ever truly operate?
premises: The discussion concerns instrumental rather than material causation.
Instrumental causes are examined for their real possibility.
No case is found where they can operate independently.
items.inference: Therefore, instrumental causes cannot be admitted as ultimately real causes.
uncertainties: The verse assumes a prior distinction between nimitta and upādāna causes.
items.plain_english: Even in the case of what is called an instrumental cause, and not a material one, instrumental causes cannot in any way be possible at any time or place.

items.question: How can the form of a beloved appear vividly in present perception?
premises: A present light or object is before the perceiver.
Memory and similar factors act as apparent instruments.
The beloved's form appears as if transferred into the present.
items.inference: The appearance of the beloved's form is occasioned by memory, not produced by an external instrumental cause.
uncertainties: ghanena may describe intensity of memory or density of appearance.
items.plain_english: For this very reason, when light is present before one, the form of the beloved may appear vividly transferred there through memory and similar instrumental triggers.

items.question: Why does a separated beloved still appear if consciousness does not go out to her?
premises: The beloved is actually separated from the perceiver.
She appears as present in consciousness.
Consciousness does not travel outward to the separated object.
items.inference: The beloved's appearance must arise within consciousness itself, not from external contact.
uncertainties: The verse is rhetorical and compressed; the opponent's view is implied.
items.plain_english: Otherwise, why would the beloved, who is actually separated, appear as present in consciousness? Consciousness does not go out in front to reach that separation.

items.question: Where do divided appearances arise in imagination and dreams?
premises: Appearances occur in imagination and dreams.
These appearances show division and distinction.
They do not require an external object present before the senses.
items.inference: There must be an inner locus in which such divided appearances clearly manifest.
uncertainties: dhīsaṃjñaṃ may be used provisionally rather than as a final doctrinal term.
items.plain_english: Therefore, let there be some inner factor called intellect, in which appearances arise clearly by division, as in imagination and in the seeing of dreams.

items.question: What truly causes the universe to appear as a reflection in consciousness?
premises: External instrumental causes have been shown to be inadequate.
The Lord possesses powers that can account for manifestation.
The universe appears in the clear sky of Bhairava-consciousness.
items.inference: The universe is a pure reflection in the Lord's consciousness, arising through his powers and not through any other agency.
uncertainties: The compound bhairavīyacidambare can be parsed in slightly different ways.
items.plain_english: Therefore, let the Lord's powers be the instrumental cause in such cases. Thus this whole universe is a pure reflection in the clear sky of Bhairava-consciousness, not by the grace of anything else.

items.question: What is the supreme power by which the Lord is the self of the universe?
premises: The Lord's power does not depend on anything else.
Through this power the Lord is the self of all.
The tradition names this power as supreme awareness.
items.inference: The Lord's independence and universal selfhood are grounded in the supreme goddess Pratibhā, the unsurpassed power.
uncertainties: Pratibhā carries both epistemic and creative connotations here.
items.plain_english: That power of the Lord, independent of anything else, by which he is the self of the universe, is declared to be the supreme, unsurpassed goddess Pratibhā.

rows.gloss: shining in the spreading of Kula

items.question: How is the supreme power related to the Lord called Akula?
premises: The Lord is named Akula.
His supreme power manifests the spreading of Kula.
The Lord is never separated from this power.
items.inference: The supreme Kaulikī power is the inseparable dynamic by which Akula manifests as Kula.
uncertainties: Akula and Kula carry technical tantric meanings not fully explicit in the verse.
items.plain_english: Of this Lord Akula, the supreme power is Kaulikī, who shines in the spreading forth of Kula; the Lord is never separated from her.

rows.gloss: that which is the pure union of those two

items.question: What is the union of Śiva and Śakti called, and why is it creative?
premises: Śiva and Śakti have a pure united form.
This union is traditionally called saṃghaṭṭa.
From this union the universe is emitted.
items.inference: The creative union of Śiva and Śakti is the power of bliss, from which the universe flows forth.
uncertainties: saṃghaṭṭa is a technical term whose full nuance depends on the tantric context.
items.plain_english: The pure united form of those two is remembered as saṃghaṭṭa. That same union is called the power of bliss, because from it the universe is emitted.

items.question: How is the goddess identified with the highest principle and creative emission?
premises: The goddess is declared to be the principle beyond supreme and non-supreme.
She is identified as the essence and heart of that reality.
The supreme emission is also identified with the Lord.
items.inference: The goddess, the heart of ultimate reality, and the supreme creative emission are presented as one sovereign reality.
uncertainties: The final identifications are compressed and may be read with doctrinal nuance.
items.plain_english: This goddess is declared to be the principle beyond the supreme and the non-supreme. She is its essence and its heart; that supreme emission is the Lord.

items.question: How is the same supreme goddess named in different tantric sources?
premises: The Devīyāmala scripture names her Kālakarṣiṇī.
The Mahāḍāmaraka rite places Śrīparā at the head.
These are presented as testimonies about the same power.
items.inference: Different tantric sources identify the same supreme goddess under distinct names and ritual roles.
uncertainties: The exact ritual sense of mastake is context-dependent.
items.plain_english: In the Devīyāmala scripture she is described as Kālakarṣiṇī, and likewise in the Mahāḍāmaraka rite the glorious supreme goddess is placed at the head.

rows.gloss: as the true nature of the mothers
that reflective awareness of being consciousness in this union

items.question: How does the Śrīpūrva scripture describe the goddess in the state of union?
premises: The Śrīpūrva scripture describes the same goddess.
She is identified with the true nature of the mothers.
In the union there is reflective awareness of being consciousness.
items.inference: The goddess is the reflective consciousness-nature present in the union and expressed as the essence of the mothers.
uncertainties: The long compound in the final token allows more than one close parsing.
items.plain_english: In the Śrīpūrva scripture she is described as the true nature of the mothers, as that reflective awareness of being consciousness within this union.

rows.gloss: by the joining of two triangles
to the state of six spokes
even in the joining of unfolding

items.question: How does the unfolding configuration return to absorption after forming a sixfold structure?
premises: Two triangles join to form a six-spoked configuration.
This occurs in the dynamic of unfolding.
The same configuration can return to absorption in its source.
items.inference: The sixfold manifestation is a phase of unfolding that can dissolve back into identity with its source.
uncertainties: The symbolic referent of the triangles is not explicit in this verse alone.
items.plain_english: When two triangles join, the configuration moves into a six-spoked state; yet even in that unfolding, it goes again into absorption in that same reality.

rows.gloss: arisen in the unfolding of will
is said also of that movement

items.question: What stirring reveals the clear form of the power of action?
premises: The power of action has a manifest form.
A stirring arises in the unfolding of will.
This stirring operates in mutual relation.
items.inference: The mutual stirring born of the unfolding of will clearly manifests the form of the power of action.
uncertainties: The exact antecedent of tadgaterapi is slightly compressed.
items.plain_english: The stirring that arises in the unfolding of will, mutually interacting, clearly manifests the form of the power of action; this is also said of that movement.

items.question: If the two powers share one form, how can unsurpassedness and bliss remain without division?
premises: The two powers are not separate in their standing.
They share the same form.
Unsurpassedness and bliss are by nature free from division.
items.inference: The apparent duality of powers does not contradict the nondual nature of unsurpassedness and bliss.
uncertainties: The verse introduces an objection that the next verse answers.
items.plain_english: Those two powers indeed share that same form and do not stand otherwise. But how can unsurpassedness and bliss, which by their own nature are free from division, appear in this way?

rows.gloss: Lord of consciousness whose nature is unlimited

items.question: How can such variegation exist within a nondual self?
premises: An objection has been raised about multiplicity within nondual bliss.
The answer appeals to the nature of the Lord of consciousness.
That Lord is unlimited in nature.
items.inference: The unlimited Lord of consciousness can contain variegation within himself without losing nonduality.
uncertainties: The verse functions as a transition into the explanation that follows.
items.plain_english: How can those two, free from division, take on such variegation within their own self? Listen: this Lord of consciousness is by nature unlimited.

rows.gloss: lord of phases of dissolution and arising of endless power-variety

items.question: What would follow if the great Lord remained in only one form?
premises: The Lord governs the arising and dissolution of endless powers.
A counterfactual is posed: remaining in one form.
Such limitation would conflict with his sovereignty.
items.inference: The Lord cannot be confined to a single form without contradicting his infinite power.
uncertainties: The verse is completed logically by the next verse.
items.plain_english: If the great Lord, master of the dissolution and arising of endless varieties of power, were to remain in only one form, then what would follow?

rows.gloss: that would abandon like a pot and such

items.question: Why would a one-form Lord lose his status as consciousness and sovereignty?
premises: Limited luminosity is the mark of inert things.
A one-form restriction would make the Lord limited.
Consciousness and sovereignty cannot belong to what is limited like a pot.
items.inference: If confined to one form, the Lord would lose both consciousness and sovereignty and become like an inert object.
uncertainties: ghaṭādivat is a standard analogy for finite objects.
items.plain_english: He would abandon his great-lordship and his nature as consciousness, like a pot or any other finite thing. For limited luminosity is indeed the defining mark of the inert.

rows.gloss: surging in the great ocean of awareness

items.question: Why must awareness express itself as many powers rather than remain limited?
premises: Awareness is distinct from the inert.
Awareness cannot be measured or limited.
The Lord's own powers arise within that awareness.
items.inference: Because awareness is unlimited, its own powers surge forth within it like waves in a great ocean.
uncertainties: The ocean-wave image is doctrinally important but metaphorical.
items.plain_english: Awareness is distinct from the inert because it cannot be measured. Therefore, his own powers surge up like waves in the great ocean of awareness.

rows.gloss: the variegation of their own self-union
the diversity of their own self-union

items.question: How do the powers produce diversity while remaining within one awareness?
premises: The powers arise like waves in awareness.
They take on variegation through their own union.
Their diversity is mutual and relational.
items.inference: The powers generate manifold diversity through their mutual self-union without departing from the one awareness.
uncertainties: svātmasaṃghaṭṭa echoes the earlier saṃghaṭṭa doctrine.
items.plain_english: Like waves, they take on the variegation of their own self-union. That mutual diversity of the powers is the diversity of their own inner union.

rows.gloss: where the three powers have become clear

items.question: What is declared to be the clear body of the power of action?
premises: The mutual diversity of powers has been described.
This diversity manifests as the power of action.
It becomes clear in a triadic abode.
items.inference: The clear body of the power of action is the manifest triadic diversity of the powers.
uncertainties: The 'fourteenth abode' is a technical reference not explained in this verse.
items.plain_english: They declare this very diversity to be the supreme, clear body of the power of action, in that fourteenth abode where the three powers have become manifest.

items.question: Why is the triadic manifestation described as a trident and as stainless?
premises: The three powers have become manifest.
The Śrīpūrva teaching calls this triśūla.
Teachers who see reality call it stainless.
items.inference: The triadic power is symbolized as a trident and recognized as stainless by authoritative teachers.
uncertainties: The symbolic mapping of the three prongs is not specified here.
items.plain_english: Therefore the Teacher declared this to be the trident in the Śrīpūrva teaching, and teachers who see reality have also called it stainless.

items.question: Why is the power-holder called stainless if will, knowledge, and action appear separately?
premises: Will, knowledge, and action appear as distinct.
The power-holder may seem affected by these distinctions.
Power itself is never truly affected by anything.
items.inference: The apparent separate affection of will, knowledge, and action does not stain the power-holder, because power is never truly affected.
uncertainties: The syntax contrasts apparent affection with ultimate unaffectedness.
items.plain_english: The power-holder seems affected because will, knowledge, and action appear separately; yet power itself is never affected by anything.

rows.gloss: by its own desired and other modes

items.question: When does the triad of will, knowledge, and action shine forth clearly as one?
premises: The triad belongs to the power-holder.
It appears through modes such as willing and so on.
The triad can appear either distinctly or in unity.
items.inference: When the triad shines forth in unity, it appears clearly as the power-holder's own integrated manifestation.
uncertainties: iṣyamāṇādikaiḥ is terse and may refer to will, knowledge, and action as modes.
items.plain_english: That same triad, through the power-holder's own modes such as willing and the rest, appears clearly; but when it shines forth in unity, then it does so as one.
